title: How Reacting Emotionally Can Ruin Your Authority
author: Michael Linsin
summary: Michael Linsin argues that one of a teacher's biggest mistakes is reacting emotionally to misbehavior, whether by glaring, lecturing, arguing, sarcasm or brooding. He says this ruins authority for four reasons: it is weak, because students see that their behavior can knock the teacher off center; it is small, because battling a student makes the teacher look petty; it is inconsistent, because it abandons the promise to follow the classroom management plan as written; and it is off-putting, because students must like and admire a teacher to follow them. Since authority and misbehavior move in opposite directions, he recommends letting the classroom management plan do the dirty work. The teacher's only job is to follow it, and in time the urge to react fades while authority and student respect grow.
points: Visible displeasure, from scowling to sarcasm, signals to even young students that misbehavior can move the teacher, which weakens authority.
Battling with a misbehaving student lowers the teacher to the student's level and reads as petty rather than strong.
Lecturing or admonishing in addition to the planned consequence breaks the promise to follow the plan as written, and inconsistency increases bad behavior and resentment.
Emotional loss of control makes the teacher less likable, and students follow leaders they admire.
The remedy is to let the management plan handle all misbehavior so the teacher's only job is consistent follow-through.
quotes: One of the biggest mistakes a teacher can make is to have an emotional reaction to misbehavior.
Like it or not, if your mood and behavior can be swayed by misbehavior, it communicates to your students that you’re not a strong leader.
Even the youngest students can recognize that outward signs of inner fragility prove that they can get under your skin and knock you off your center.
Lowering yourself to a misbehaving student’s level by battling with them or showing how they hurt your feelings makes you appear petty.
You promised to follow your classroom management plan as written. Period. If you lecture or admonish instead, or even in addition to, you’re going back on your word.
The solution is to allow your classroom management plan to do your dirty work for you. Let it handle all misbehavior.
In time and with consistency, the urge to react will go away. The result is that your authority will rise and your students will view you as a leader worth following.
